title: Asymmetric property visibility
summary: PHP 8.4 lets a typed property declare a write visibility stricter than its read visibility - most commonly `public private(set) Type $prop` - so external code can read the property but only the declaring class (or, with protected(set), a subclass) can write it, replacing a private backing property plus a public getter written solely to expose read access.
new_code_policy: On a feature ceiling of 8.4 or above, replace a private backing property plus a public getter written solely to expose read-only access with a single asymmetric-visibility property declaration (`public private(set) Type $prop`, or the bare `private(set) Type $prop` shorthand, whose read visibility defaults to public). Never emit `private(set)`/`protected(set)` at all while the feature ceiling is 8.3 or lower: it is a parse error there, not merely an unsupported runtime construct, so it fails to parse the entire file, not just the one declaration.
existing_code_policy: Do not bulk-convert every private-property-plus-getter pair to asymmetric visibility. Migrate one only when it is already being touched for another reason, and only after confirming the feature ceiling is 8.4 or newer, since introducing this syntax on a lower ceiling does not degrade gracefully - the whole file fails to parse, not just the touched property. A set-restricted property is also a genuine public-API change for any code outside the declaring class (and, for protected(set), outside its subclasses) that currently writes to the property directly; every such external write site must be found and moved onto the class's own API before the migration is safe.
guideline: Once the feature ceiling reaches PHP 8.4, prefer asymmetric property visibility (`public private(set) Type $prop`, or the bare `private(set) Type $prop` shorthand for the common public-read/private-write case) over a private property paired with a public getter written only to expose read access. Never emit `private(set)`/`protected(set)` while the feature ceiling is 8.3 or below, since it is a parse error there.
details: PHP 8.4 implemented asymmetric property visibility (RFC asymmetric-visibility-v2); the official UPGRADING text records it in one line: "Implemented asymmetric property visibility." The feature lets a typed property declare two visibilities instead of one: a read visibility, and, via a second modifier written as `private(set)` or `protected(set)`, a write visibility that must be equal to or more restrictive than the read visibility (the engine rejects the reverse at compile time with "Visibility of property ... must not be weaker than set visibility"). `public private(set) string $id` reads as public from anywhere but writes only from inside the declaring class; `public protected(set) int $balance` reads as public but writes only from the declaring class or a subclass. Writing only the set-modifier, e.g. bare `private(set) string $id`, is shorthand for `public private(set) string $id`: the read visibility defaults to public whenever no explicit read visibility is given. A write-restricted property is not readonly: from inside its allowed write scope it can be assigned as many times as ordinary code needs - verified locally on PHP 8.4.19, a `protected(set)` property accepted two separate writes from a method on the declaring class and accumulated normally - and only a write attempted from outside that scope raises an Error ("Cannot modify private(set) property Class::$prop from global scope"), whereas a `readonly` property (also verified locally) rejects every write after its first, including a second write attempted from inside its own declaring class ("Cannot modify readonly property Class::$prop"). Asymmetric visibility requires an explicit property type - an untyped property carrying a set-visibility modifier is a compile-time fatal error, confirmed locally ("Property with asymmetric visibility ... must have type") - and is available on constructor-promoted properties using the same syntax (e.g. `public function __construct(public private(set) float $x) {}`), also confirmed locally. On any feature ceiling below 8.4, `private(set)`/`protected(set)` are new tokens the parser does not recognize in this position: using this syntax on PHP 8.3 or earlier is a parse error that fails the whole file, not a runtime warning confined to one property, so this construct must never be emitted unless the feature ceiling is already 8.4 or above. Asymmetric visibility for static properties is a separate, later addition: PHP 8.5 added it (UPGRADING-8.5.0, "2. New Features" -> Core: "Added asymmetric visibility support for static properties.") and it remains unavailable on 8.4, confirmed locally ("Static property may not have asymmetric visibility"); that static-only extension is out of this rule's scope, which covers only the instance-property feature introduced in 8.4, and is documented separately by the `language.static_asymmetric_visibility` rule.
notes: A write-restricted property is not readonly: verified locally on PHP 8.4.19, a private(set)/protected(set) property accepts any number of writes from inside its allowed write scope and only rejects a write attempted from outside it ("Cannot modify private(set) property Class::$prop from global scope"), whereas a readonly property rejects every write after its first, even a second write attempted from inside its own declaring class ("Cannot modify readonly property Class::$prop").

Asymmetric visibility requires an explicit property type; an untyped property with a set-visibility modifier is a compile-time fatal error ("Property with asymmetric visibility ... must have type"), confirmed locally on PHP 8.4.19.

Static properties could not use asymmetric visibility on 8.4 at all (confirmed locally: "Static property may not have asymmetric visibility"); PHP 8.5 added that support separately (UPGRADING-8.5.0.txt, '2. New Features' -> Core: "Added asymmetric visibility support for static properties."). That static-only extension is out of this rule's scope, which covers only instance properties as introduced in 8.4, and is documented separately by the language.static_asymmetric_visibility rule.
Evidence: UPGRADING-8.4.0.txt, '2. New Features' -> Core: "Implemented asymmetric property visibility."
